explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says the cloud “…appeared like fire above the tabernacle from evening until morning.” I'd have had a hard time sleeping under that one. Daytime, a cloud. Night, a glow.

Smoke is a fair guess when you hear "cloud," but the text never says smoke. It says the cloud “…appeared like fire above the tabernacle from evening until morning.” So at night the people looked up and saw something like fire sitting over the Tent.

Lightning shows up, flashes and is gone before you finish saying "whoa." The text says the cloud “…appeared like fire…” and that it stayed that way continually (Numbers 9:16). Nobody in that camp had to wait for a flash to see it.
Not quite, friend. The text says it remained that way continually. The cloud would cover the tabernacle by day, and at night it would appear like fire. It wasn't a one day visit, it kept showing up.

Right. The text says the cloud “…remained that way continually; the cloud would cover the tabernacle by day, and at night it would appear like fire.” It was there day and night. Some guests leave after one visit, but this cloud stayed around.

That's it, baker. Verse 17 says, “Whenever the cloud was lifted from above the Tent, the Israelites would set out…” Cloud goes up, camp gets packed. Packing up a whole camp takes a lot of work, and I can barely close one cookie box without my mustache getting tangled.

Good thought, but the text says something else here. When the cloud was lifted from above the Tent, the Israelites would set out. The lifting was their sign to move. Gathering is a different thing that comes later in the passage.

Waiting is what they do when the cloud stays put. Verse 18 says, “As long as the cloud remained over the tabernacle, they remained encamped.” But the question is about the cloud lifting. When it lifts, they set out.
Yes! The text says, “…wherever the cloud settled, there the Israelites would camp.” The cloud picks the spot, and the people unpack right there. No map and no vote, just a cloud landing.

The text doesn't say the cloud vanishes. It says wherever the cloud settled, there the Israelites would camp. The cloud is still there, sitting over the Tent. A cloud that disappeared would leave them with no idea where to unpack, and I'd panic.

Nothing in the text says the cloud darkens. What it says is that “…wherever the cloud settled, there the Israelites would camp.” The key word is settled. The cloud lands, and that's where the camp goes.

That's right. Verse 18 says, “At the LORD’s command the Israelites set out, and at the LORD’s command they camped.” Both the going and the stopping came from Him. Verse 23 says it again, so the writer clearly wanted this one to stick.

Aaron comes up later in this passage, since his sons are the priests who sound the trumpets (Numbers 10:8). But for setting out and camping, the text says it was the LORD's command. Aaron isn't named in this part.

No committee here, friend. Verse 18 says, “At the LORD’s command the Israelites set out, and at the LORD’s command they camped.” Nobody had to hold a meeting about whether to move. The text puts the command with the LORD.

Not this time. The text says, “Even when the cloud lingered over the tabernacle for many days, the Israelites kept the LORD’s charge and did not set out.” So no moving on without the cloud. They stayed put, many days or not.

Right. Verse 19 says they “…kept the LORD’s charge and did not set out.” Many days of the same view out the tent door, and they stayed anyway. I spent years in the same drawer, so I know about waiting, but they had a cloud to look at.

Yes, baker. Verse 21 says, “Whether it was by day or by night, when the cloud was taken up, they would set out.” Night doesn't change anything. I can only imagine the packing in the dark, and I wouldn't trust my mustache with a tent stake.

That sounds sensible to me too, but the text says something different. “Whether it was by day or by night, when the cloud was taken up, they would set out.” The lifting is the signal, whatever time it is. No sunrise needed.

The text doesn't mention scouts anywhere in this passage. It says, “Whether it was by day or by night, when the cloud was taken up, they would set out.” The cloud lifting was enough for them. They moved when it moved.

True! Verse 23 says, “They camped at the LORD’s command, and they set out at the LORD’s command; they carried out the LORD’s charge according to His command through Moses.” Moses, Israel's leader, was the one it came through, and the people did it. That's the whole picture in one verse.

It's actually true, friend. Verse 23 says they carried out the LORD's charge “…according to His command through Moses.” The command came through Moses, and the Israelites carried it out. Both halves of the statement match the text.

explanations.answer: Calling the people and moving camp
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says to make two trumpets of hammered silver “…to be used for calling the congregation and for having the camps set out.” Two jobs for two trumpets. That's better than my old drawer, where nothing had a job at all.
A new king is a fun guess, but nothing in these verses says that. The LORD says the trumpets are for calling the congregation and for having the camps set out. That's their job here.

The text doesn't mention a storm. The LORD gives the trumpets a clear job: “…for calling the congregation and for having the camps set out.” Later they're sounded in battle and on joyous occasions (Numbers 10:9-10). A storm isn't on the list.

Close, but that's the one trumpet rule. When both are sounded, “…the whole congregation is to assemble before you at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” The whole congregation, not just the leaders. Both trumpets means everybody comes.

Right. Verse 3 says, “When both are sounded, the whole congregation is to assemble before you at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” Only one trumpet gathers the leaders (Numbers 10:4). Two trumpets, whole crowd.

Yes! Verse 4 says, “…then the leaders, the heads of the clans of Israel, are to gather before you.” One trumpet gets the leaders, and two get everybody. Simple system, and I like simple. My bakery has one oven mitt and I still lose it.

The priests do show up in this passage, but as the ones blowing the trumpets. “The sons of Aaron, the priests, are to sound the trumpets” (Numbers 10:8). The ones who gather at one trumpet are the leaders, the heads of the clans.
The text doesn't call them servants. Verse 4 says the leaders are “…the heads of the clans of Israel.” Those are the ones who gather before Moses when only one trumpet sounds.

That's right. Verse 6 says, “When you sound the short blasts a second time, the camps that lie on the south side are to set out.” East goes first, and south follows on the second round of short blasts. Everybody waits for their turn.

It's actually true, friend. Verse 6 says, “When you sound the short blasts a second time, the camps that lie on the south side are to set out.” First short blasts send the east side (Numbers 10:5), and the second round sends the south.

Yes! Verse 7 says, “To convene the assembly, you are to sound long blasts, not short ones.” Short is for setting out, and long is for gathering. Mix them up, and I'd be standing around holding a tent stake.

Battle does use trumpets, but with short blasts. Verse 9 says, “When you enter into battle in your land against an adversary who attacks you, sound short blasts on the trumpets…” The long blasts are for convening the assembly (Numbers 10:7).
The text doesn't tie any blast to taking down the tent. Short blasts are what have the camps set out. The long blasts are for convening the assembly.

True! The LORD says that when they sound short blasts in battle, “…you will be remembered before the LORD your God and saved from your enemies.” (Numbers 10:9) That's His own promise. The trumpets go with it.
It's actually true, friend. Verse 9 says that when they sound short blasts in battle, “…you will be remembered before the LORD your God and saved from your enemies.” The LORD is the one who says it.

Yes! Verse 10 says the trumpets blown over the offerings are “…to serve as a reminder for you before your God.” Joyous occasions, feasts, the start of every month. I need a timer to remember a batch is in the oven, and they got silver trumpets.

The text doesn't call it a warning. On joyous occasions, appointed feasts and the start of each month, the trumpets “…serve as a reminder for you before your God.” These are happy occasions. A reminder is what the verse says.
Nothing in the text calls the trumpets a payment. They're blown over the burnt offerings and peace offerings “…to serve as a reminder for you before your God.” The word in the verse is reminder.
